title: Bangladesh's Measles Death Toll Crosses 1,000 as Outbreak Rages On
excerpt: Six months after it began, Bangladesh's measles outbreak — the largest in the world, per the CDC — has killed more than 1,000 people, nearly all children, as vaccination gaps and a faltering immunization program fuel the spread.
body:
• Bangladesh's measles outbreak, now in its sixth month, has killed more than 1,000 people — nearly all of them children — according to government and media tallies.
  • The U.S. CDC ranks it the world's largest current measles outbreak, with Bangladesh recording 57,561 infections in the first half of 2026, ahead of India at 26,332.
  • Experts blame vaccination gaps in 2024 and 2025, procurement changes under the interim government, and an error that left about 4.6 million children out of the vaccination campaign.
  • Around 1,000 children are still being hospitalized daily; experts say vaccination must be extended to at least age 15 to stop transmission.

Six months after it began, Bangladesh's measles outbreak has crossed a grim milestone: more than 1,000 confirmed and suspected measles-related deaths, the world's largest current outbreak, with no sign of infections declining.

The Business Standard reported that the combined tally of confirmed and suspected deaths reached 1,002, including 100 laboratory-confirmed fatalities. Reuters, citing the same health ministry figures on Sept. 9, put the toll at 999 deaths, with more than 146,000 suspected patients hospitalized since the outbreak emerged in March. The government's Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) recorded 167,580 suspected measles cases by early September, including nearly 20,000 laboratory-confirmed infections.

Context & Background

The outbreak follows years of progress toward measles elimination. Bangladesh maintained measles vaccination coverage at or above the 95 percent level recommended by the WHO for much of the past decade, apart from a decline during the COVID-19 pandemic, Reuters reported. But the country missed its measles elimination target because of vaccination gaps in 2024 and 2025, said Professor Mahmudur Rahman, an epidemiologist, former director of the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR), and chair of the National Verification Committee for Measles and Rubella Elimination.

Health Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain told parliament that procurement policy changes had triggered a vaccine shortage, while the postponement of a vaccination program in 2024 and the cancellation of a nationwide measles-rubella campaign in 2025 left more children vulnerable. A government vaccination drive launched in April targeted about 18 million children aged six months to five years and claimed 103 percent coverage — but a vitamin A campaign in June covered 22.6 million children in the same age group, suggesting roughly 4.6 million children were left out of the measles program because the target population was set too low, public health expert Dr M Mushtuq Husain told The Business Standard.

"To my knowledge, Bangladesh has never witnessed so many children dying from measles. Nor have we ever seen such a high number of patients in a single year. This is a truly terrible situation, and the saddest part is that the victims are children."

— Prof Mahmudur Rahman, epidemiologist and former IEDCR director

Impact & Analysis

The toll is still rising daily. The Business Standard reported three more children died from measles and measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours to 8 a.m. on Sept. 6, taking the combined tally to 994 at the time. Around 1,000 children are still being hospitalized every day on average, with four to six dying daily — and there has not been a single day without a measles-related death in six months.

Children under five accounted for about 80 percent of cases in the early stages, but epidemiologists now say the infection has spread across nearly all child age groups. Prof Rahman told The Business Standard there is no sign of cases declining, and that vaccination should be extended beyond age five to at least age 15, with evidence-based campaigns targeted at the hardest-hit areas. The DGHS says it has a plan to expand the vaccination age range, but no final decision has been made. Under WHO guidelines, both confirmed and epidemiologically linked probable cases count as measles — a point experts stress, because some deaths are being attributed to pneumonia without measles being recorded as the underlying cause.

Diaspora Angle

Bangladesh's large diaspora in the United States, Britain, and Canada — and families planning travel to South Asia — should note the CDC ranking puts Bangladesh first globally for measles cases this year, with India second; checking MMR vaccination status before travel is the simplest precaution.

What's Next

The government launched an emergency vaccination drive in March with the WHO, UNICEF, and the Gavi vaccine alliance, later expanding it nationwide in phases. Public health experts say controlling the outbreak now requires closing immunity gaps, extending vaccination to older children, stepping up community-level surveillance, and rebuilding the program oversight that experts say weakened after the political transition. Until then, they warn, the death count will keep climbing.
